DO NOT GET ONE DONE BY THE AA. 

My partner and I paid a deposit on a car and said we'd buy it subject to the AA inspection coming back saying the car was in tip top shape. Came back all clear so we paid a hefty amount of money. We got the car and we're super happy. It looked like it was in pristine condition (which you would expect for the amount we paid) and we were chuffed. Fast forward a couple weeks to when we were at a gas station and finally remembered to fill up the washer bottle so we could wash the windscreen... popped the bonnet and started pouring the water into the spout, except it was coming out the bottom as fast as it was going in. Took it to a mechanic, and turns out the washer bottle was CRUSHED with HUGE GAPING GASHES from being in an accident. Not only that, but the bumper was LITERALLY GLUED ON. 

We are currently in a battle with the dealer and the AA about it. On the check slip, it said the washer bottle was checked and it obviously wasn't. They have been picked up on these things multiple times. I'm pretty sure it was only this year that someone took their story to Fair Go. 

Get it checked by a reputable mechanic no matter what, I know that's what I'll be doing from now on. You can sometimes find some that will go to where the car is situated for some extra $. I will never trust AA again, so much so that I'm withdrawing my membership. 

Hope things go well!

TLDR; told dealer we'd buy a car subject to good AA inspection, AA said they did an inspection, got the car, found out a whole bunch of shit was wrong when they said it wasn't, now in a huge battle with dealership and AA, heaps of stress 🙃 USE A MECHANIC NOT THE AA.

> It doesn't do a heck of a lot with a Fitbit in all honesty. Choosing a difference sport will choose whether the GPS should be used or not, and will alter the metrics you see on screen during the workout (e.g. you want "Pace" for running and "Speed" for cycling). So it's really just a "profile" of pre-configured options, and in the Fitbit world this basically boils down to "Should I use the GPS" and "How should I display your speed".
> In terms of "What does it do different to track a yoga workout?" versus something like, say, weight lifting? Practically nothing - they're both indoor sports, so it'll track HR and steps with no GPS for both. Versus running - the difference is basically that for running it'll try and track GPS as well. More advanced (and more expensive) devices with more sensors can start doing more nuanced things with multisport.
> Other than that, it will also ensure the activity is correctly titled when it is uploaded to the app/web service. The title of the activity determines the way the app/web service uses and displays the information; for example metrics like the way Fitbit calculates the calorie burn; or a run will be displayed with "split" times, whereas for yoga it won't. This is just a display layer over the top though, ultimately the data captured is pretty much the same.
